segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A friend in South Africa sent me the link to this article that is making the rounds there. It's an open letter, supposedly from the foreign media, to every man, woman, and child in their country.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It begins, "Dear South Africa, please get the F of the way. Wait, that probably came out wrong. As you may have noted, we're back!" Meaning of course, that the foreign press has returned to South Africa to cover what is happening now with Nelson Mandela. I'll go back to the letter.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: "In the real world, far away from your sleepy backwater, news works on a 24-hour cycle, and you need to get out of the way. It's nothing personal. In fact, we couldn't do this successfully without you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In many cases, our footage is made more compelling by your presence. Specifically, we are fond of small black children praying and slash or singing in unison. Equally telegenic are the Aryan ubermensch blond kids, also praying slash singing, who help underscore the theme that Mandela united people of all races under a rainbow umbrella.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Also very important, thematically speaking, are Mandela's successors. We very much like the idea that your ex-president was quote, 'one of a kind', and that despite his best efforts, the current batch of idiots proved that he was an exceptional presence. Sui generis. And we don't have to worry about someone else like him coming along in Africa ever again.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We enjoy your leaders' bumbling ways, their daft nonsequiturs. This story would lack a tragic arc without Jacob Zuma." That of course, is the current president of the country. "May he keep on keeping on."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The letter continues. "Then there's the Mandela family. Really, where would we derive our soap operatic undertones if it weren't for the infighting and blinged-up brashness of that clan? We love subtly implying that a saint sired a generation of professional shoppers, no-goodniks.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In our biz we call that irony. Makes for great copy. In fact, we love everything about the country that doesn't live up to Mandela's legacy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We will take every opportunity to mention how everything you do flies in the face of everything Mandela would have wanted for his people, how you're basically a nation of underachieving screw ups. All of this is fantastic. We thank you profusely for your individual and collective contributions to this essential storyline, and urge you to keep squandering your potential."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Can I say what I love about this? It was written by a journalist named Richard Poplak for the South African news service Daily Maverick, which you can find online.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What I love about this is how it doesn't just take us foreigners inside how a South African might see our news coverage and the tone of that coverage, it also reveals a world of utterly justified resentments that I guess maybe we could have suspected, but we didn't really know about. It is an insider's view totally.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, today on our radio show, we have stories from three radically different locations. We dive into three very different worlds for the insider's view that only insiders have.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life, distributed by Public Radio International. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, The Weeds of Discontent. What we have now is a recording of a very unusual conversation that came about in an unusual way.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's this filmmaker named Eugene Jarecki who made a documentary about prisons and the criminal justice system called The House I Live In . And he's been taking it around the country and showing it in prisons, kind of Johnny Cash style, for inmates and corrections staff.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of our producers, Brian Reed, went to one of those screenings, which is where this conversation happened. Here's Brian.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: The screening I saw was at Joseph Harp Correctional Center, a medium security prison in Lexington, Oklahoma. About 35 inmates, most of them in for drug related crimes or with a history of drug use, sat waiting in the visiting room in chairs facing a projector screen.

segments.speaker: Prison Guard
segments.text: Once we get to where we're getting ready to start the movie, if you're here, you're staying.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: More than a dozen staff members came to watch the movie too, including the warden and some state officials from the Oklahoma Department of Corrections. And before the screening started, what did these drug offenders think the movie was going to be about?

segments.speaker: Prisoner 1
segments.text: Rehab.

segments.speaker: Prisoner 2
segments.text: Probably about some drugs and how to prevent yourself from doing some drugs.

segments.speaker: Prisoner 3
segments.text: How drugs is bad for you. How it mess up your skin and your body. Make you age quicker too.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: But these guys were way off base. The House I Live In is about how drugs are bad for them, but not in the way they were expecting.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Because it argues that the war on drugs has completely failed. That it's made law enforcement less effective and overwhelmed prisons. That's it's a self-perpetuating system which preys on poor, uneducated people. A system where politicians win elections by being tough on crime, a multi-billion dollar industry and entire towns thrive off the business of incarceration, and laws trap people with few opportunities in a cycle of committing crimes.

segments.speaker: Charles Ogletree
segments.text: People don't realize, for example, that when you arrest a young black man and he goes to jail, when he gets out of the prison, he can't get a job in most places because of his record.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: This is Charles Ogletree, a professor at Harvard Law School.

segments.speaker: Charles Ogletree
segments.text: If he wants to go back to school to go to college, he's ineligible by law for certain grants. He can't get certain health care benefits. His family that was the centerpiece of his life, if they're living in public housing, they can't take him in. He can't vote!

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: The film has interviews with people throughout the criminal justice system. Inmates and their families, but also judges, police officers, and prison staff. Almost all of them say, in some way or another, that the system needs to be fixed.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: And what made it even more interesting for this audience in Oklahoma is that several people from the Oklahoma Department of Corrections are in the movie. And a couple of them were at the screening, watching it with the prisoners. Like Mike Carpenter, who oversees security for Oklahoma's medium security prisons.

segments.speaker: Mike Carpenter
segments.text: I am very much a law and order kind of guy. I would rather have 10 police cars than 1 soup kitchen if you give me the choice. But sometimes I think that we need to be smarter about what those police officers are actually out there doing.

segments.speaker: Mike Carpenter
segments.text: I think sometimes we have people doing a whole lot of time for not very much crime. It's almost like they're paying for our fear, instead of paying for their crime.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: So when the screening was over, some of the inmates were surprised that prison staff had even shown them this at all. One guy said it was exhilarating to hear corrections officers say things like, "We're jailing too many people. We're locking them up for too long."

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: So we had this idea. We thought the film might prompt a conversation that prisoners and guards don't normally get to have about the prison system. And Oklahoma corrections authorities agreed to give us a room where I could sit down prisoners and guards and they could talk to each other one on one.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Who do you want to talk to? Who do you want to talk with?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I want to talk to Dooley and Shelock.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: OK. Why do you want to talk to them?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: My own personal opinions.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: This is Antwaun Wells. He's 25, serving the third year of a nine year sentence for shooting a guy during an argument and also for stealing TVs from a Target and then stabbing a security guard in the arm on the way out of the store.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: It's not his first time in prison. He'd been in before. One of the staff members he picked-- Shelock-- wasn't around. But Dooley was.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Dooley is Lt. Cecil Dooley. He's been a corrections officer for 14 years. He's a big burly guy. He wasn't there to see the movie. He was the guard on duty supervising the inmates as they watched the film.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I recorded other conversations throughout the day. But this was the one that stood out.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: We're going to go in here. Pardon me, guys. We got our first pair. We'll see how this goes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Lt. Dooley and Antwaun sat down facing each other. I sat off to the side to try and stay out of their way.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now let me say here that this whole thing was a total experiment. I don't think any of us knew what to expect. And just to get in front of this, Antwaun did not bring Dooley in here to talk about the movie.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: All right, so you wanted to bring him in here and ask him a question.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Yep.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Do you have your question?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I want to know why y'all feel that it's so important for y'all to demand respect, but don't want to give it.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: When you say "y'all," you putting everybody in the same boat.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Well, I can't put everyone in the same boat, because there is some guards that are respectful. But it's some-- being you in particular with me-- I feel that you're just disrespectful.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Like the other day in the office, I asked you to come here. If you was to ask me to come here and I told you to hold on, you'd have wrote me up because I didn't follow a direct order.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I acknowledged you. I told you to hold on.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I [INAUDIBLE].

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Unless you're bleeding, dying, or giving birth, the stuff that I had going on was much more important than what you needed at that time.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I just feel--

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I've never once called you outside of your name.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: No, that's--

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I've never slandered you in any way.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Yeah. No. And I'm not gonna say that and I never will say that incident happened. But what I'm saying is that's not the only--

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: But you come in here and you say I was disrespectful because you don't get what you want when you want it.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: In my eyes, I feel like you and other guards view us as if we're nothing. Y'all walk round with y'all head held up. You know what I'm saying?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: It's always, y'all win. No matter what the situation is, y'all win. You have a arrogant attitude. Your attitude is I'm Dooley. I'm big bad Dooley.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: If I tell you to do something that's not illegal, that's not going to jeopardize your life, that's not offensive, you should have no problem doing it. Whether you like it or not is a totally different story.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: That's where the disrespect come in. Because you had--

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: That's not disrespectful.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: OK, you had me pick up dandelions.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Just to prove a point to me. To prove a point that y'all have power.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: OK. So you're still upset over the dandelion deal?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Yes, I really am. That really actually frustrated me.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: If you wouldn't have bucked up against that officer that day--

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: But see, that's what I'm saying. You never came and asked me exactly what happened.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Don't need to.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Exactly. You took your officer's word and you left it at that. It's always three sides to each story. My side, his side, and the truth.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: You left two sides out and you went off of what your officer said. You never came to me as a man and asked me. You know what I'm saying?

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I did.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: And then you forced me to do something just because you could. And if I didn't, you threatened to ship me.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Antwaun is saying Lt. Dooley threatened to ship him to another prison.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I don't remember threatening to ship you. But I could.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Yes, you threatened to ship me.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I could. Disobedience to order.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Exactly. And you told me trying to override your staff, you could ship me.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Mm hmm. I could.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: And if I didn't pick up dandelions,  you'll put me in a holding cell.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: And if I remember correctly, that was over you trying to get other people to stand up against that officer and not do what he was telling you to do.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: No. That's exactly what I'm  saying.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: So OK, sure. They weren't talking about the history of the drug war or the prison industrial complex or any of the other big ideas from the movie.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: But it was interesting to listen to them argue like this. It was intimate. It was personal. They were bickering like family members. Like a dad and his kid going at it.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: And I felt like I was seeing something people on the outside don't usually have the opportunity to see. You realize, oh, right, these two are embedded in each other's lives in a way that only happens when one person has the power to punish the other and the other person has a whole lot of time to stew over it.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: And the thing that was bugging Antwaun, the dandelions, seems small, but kind of gets to the heart of what he hates about being incarcerated. And he wanted to hash that out with Dooley.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Obviously, there's disagreement about what happened that day, which was months ago, by the way. Antwaun says another officer had given some other inmates a few tasks to do, like pick up trash. Antwaun went up to the other inmates and told them they were allowed to do the tasks in a different order than the guard did.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Dooley says that's not how it happened. That Antwaun Wells was telling other inmates to disobey a guard. So Dooley gave him what they call extra duty. In this case, to pick dandelions.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I don't--

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Was it hard?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: No. I mean, it wasn't hard. It was just--

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Did it take a lot of time?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: No. It didn't take a lot of time. It's still the principle. You made me--

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Did you break any bones?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: No. You could have said, go pick up some trash. You specifically made me pick up a flower that grows out the ground.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Mm hmm.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Just because you could.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Exactly. It's always going to be officers that feel like just because I have the power and authority, I can do and say what I want to to these people.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: There wasn't just to put power and authority. I am where I am because I have morals, ethics, and beliefs that I stand by.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Still yet even once again--

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I think your problem, Mr. Wells, is you like to dwell on the fact that you don't get your way each and every time. And that's part of the reason that you're in prison--

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: No, it's not.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: --is because you like to buck the system.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I'm in prison 'cause I shot somebody. I'll never deny that fact.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I'm in prison because I put myself here.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I made the choices in my life because I chose to.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: And those are poor decisions.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I don't blame nobody for nothing that happens. But when I feel that's just like there's some guards here that's just rude for no reason. I don't understand that.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: You didn't care enough about me to even ask me my opinion. You didn't care enough about nothing that I had going on, once again, because I'm an inmate. Y'all feel just because I came to the penitentiary, that I have no rights.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: You being an offender has nothing to do with it. 'Cause you have no say over anything.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Policy and procedure.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: You have no say to tell my officer what he can and cannot do, to ask people to do.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Exactly. That's the point where you're missing. I told the inmates that. I didn't tell the officer nothing.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Right. Which makes you the person that was instigating.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: They went on like this for more than 20 minutes.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I know you don't like me, just like I don't like you.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I've never disrespected you and my job has nothing to do with like or dislike.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: You disrespected me that day that you didn't ask me my side of the story and you made me pick up dandelions--

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: That's not disrespect.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Because you could.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: That's not disrespect.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: You power abused because you could. You just admitted it.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: It's not even abuse of power.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Finally I interrupted and asked them what they thought about the movie we just watched. Dooley had actually seen it before. He had it recorded on his DVR. And he liked it.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: He told me that for several years now, he's felt that the country needs to rethink the way it does corrections. He said he often tells inmates that when they get down to the last three years or so of their sentence, he thinks they should be released early.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: When you see that movie and when you think about your day to day, are you dissatisfied? Are you frustrated with the system, where it's gotten?

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Absolutely. Absolutely.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: What frustrates you most?

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: The fact that we have now taken people and made them a monetary commodity. Right now the big thing is the push to privatization. To make money off of prisons, to make money off of people's lives, to make money to incarcerate people. That to me, seems backwards.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: He turned to Antwaun for a second.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: And this is not to push your button or anything like that. I did more in 10 seconds of his life by making him pick up dandelions. He will remember the fact that I came up there and I told him to pick dandelions for arguing with an officer. He will remember that forever.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: And if that one issue makes him hate me to the point where he doesn't ever want to put himself in that position again, then I have done my job. I've done my job to correct an action forever.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: What do you think of that, Antwaun? You get that?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I mean, I understand it. But I still don't feel that it's fair.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Penitentiary to me is just slavery in another form. In my eyes, these is my owners and I have to do what they say, otherwise I have consequences. Just like the slave master. You either do what he say or you get punished.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Then the conversation got more personal. Lt. Dooley told Antwaun that the last time he got out of prison he had a chance to stay out, to make a different life for himself. But instead he re-offended.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Antwaun said he didn't have many options. And it was around this point that Antwaun and Dooley actually started to hear each other out a bit.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: What was I supposed to do? I come from the hood. I come from nothing. You tell me, what was I supposed to do?

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Now you're talking outside my purview, because I don't know where you're from.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Exactly. Exactly. You don't know where I'm from. And I don't feel that you would care.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Me as a person, if I didn't have all the tattoos or whatever, if I had the money to get them removed, you could put me in a white collar neighborhood and I could make it because I have a education. You know what I'm saying? I have two years of college.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I have no other option but to accept my choices I made. You know what I'm saying? I do admit my failures. You know what  I'm saying?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: But I will say that there were obstacles that at that time, I didn't think right of overcoming, so I chose the wrong way to overcome them.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: You know what? I grew up very poor. I didn't know I was poor. My mom always had two different jobs growing up. I was taking care of my little brother at the age of eight by myself.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I'm on this side, you're on that side. That's all decisions. And you know the difference between right and wrong.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: But you make the conscious decision to continue doing the same things and expect different results.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Sometimes you get pinned in a corner and you're forced to do what you know. Like when I got out of the penitentiary this time, for three days I wore the same clothes until I went out and had to steal me some clothes. My sister and my brother and my mama didn't give me no handout. You know what I'm saying?

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Jobs, they won't-- you're a felon. You know what I'm saying? I applied for 35 jobs with my little brother. And just because both of us is felons, we got nowhere.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: So what am I gonna do? I'm going to go commit a crime, make me some money, and then go get me a dope sack.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: See, if I were to go, the first thing I would do would try to go pick up a lawn mower or something and go mow some lawns. That's the difference in thought.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Yeah. That was an option. But still, yeah, once again, where am I gonna get the lawn mower from?

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I got friends.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: I feel like society made a lot of rules to keep people safe. But at the same time, the people that they was trying to keep safe from, they gave us no other option but to go back out and re-offend because they put so many limitations on what we could do that where you have no other option but to go back to what you used to do.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: I've heard that same story for 14 years. I don't know how to fix it. If I did, I'd be a millionaire. If I did, there wouldn't be people in prison because I could tell them how to fix it.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: That conversation took place about a month and a half ago. And since then, I've wondered if it changed anything for Antwaun and Lt. Dooley, if it improved their relationship at all. So I called them up the other day to ask them.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I talked to Dooley first and he said he'd only run into Antwaun a couple times since they'd talked. So he hadn't really noticed a difference.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: But he did come down here. And when I called him down for this interview, he didn't have that same negative attitude he normally did.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Dooley said he hadn't thought much about the conversation since it happened. And when I asked him if it changed him at all, if he felt more sympathetic towards Antwaun or if he thought differently now about the way he disciplines inmates, he said no. Not at all. Then he went to get Antwaun.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Now hold on just a second.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: [PHONE RINGING]

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: Are you still there?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I am.

segments.speaker: Lt. Cecil Dooley
segments.text: If you'll have a seat right there, Mr. Wells. This is the gentleman that did our interview while we were in the room when they came and showed the video. Here he is.

segments.speaker: Antwaun Wells
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And while the columns are not explicitly political, he's a minority in Israel. He's an Arab who is also an Israeli citizen. Which, as you might expect, is complicated.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A few years ago, Kashua and his wife and kids moved from East Jerusalem-- where most of the Arabs in the city live-- to West Jerusalem, where it's almost all Jews, no Arabs. And that kind of blew people's minds, including his.

segments.text: He and his wife made the move to get a better apartment in a neighborhood that had better services. But the move was radical in a country where even middle class and rich Arab Israelis do not usually live among Jews, especially in Jerusalem.

segments.text: Don't get me wrong. I can be a real jerk, but I do love my wife. Today more than ever.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I've mentioned before that our apartment suddenly started to get on her nerves. At first there were trivial comments like, "These shower hooks are really annoying," or "There's not even a proper place for the shoe closet," even though we never had a shoe closet.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: The complaints gathered momentum after our third child was born. "I think we need another room for the baby." "We have to paint. Have you seen the walls? They're already black from the kids' hands."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: Very quickly, the home that I loved so much, in the building I love, in the neighborhood I love became a nightmare. So I asked my wife, "What do you say to renovating?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I don't know how or why, but of the three renovating teams who were bidding to just basically build a plaster wall and paint the place, I found myself choosing the team that gave me a price three times higher than that of any of the others, an Ashkenazi architect with a Mizrahi interior designer. Maybe it was the iPad that the interior designer used when he presented the work plan. Or maybe it was just because every time he said "plaster wall, " he added the adjective "designer."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I closed the deal with the Ashkenazi, who promised to go with my wife to all the stores to choose the color of the designer plaster wall, pick out the shoe closet, and find the hooks that best suited her needs. Because the most important thing in interior design is for the house to meet your needs, said the interior designer, pointing at my wife.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "14,000 shekels for a paint job!" my father shouted at me. "For what? On every electricity pole there is a sign, paint your home for 1,800 shekels."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "What 1,800 shekels?" I said. "And anyway, we're talking about designer paint, Dad!"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: My father still lives in the village where I grew up, Tira. He tried to explain to me that I'm an imbecile. That in Tira, you could get a new shower and a paint job with a plaster wall, even a designer one, for a tenth of the price.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I tried to explain to him that I don't live in Tira, that the interior designer promised that the finished work would last a lifetime. And that anyway, there was nothing that could be done about it. Life in West Jerusalem in my neighborhood costs a little more, with all due respect to Tira.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "You're a dunce," my father concluded. "Do what you like."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I felt like making coffee. At least I wanted to, but the milk frother in the machine-- which you have to belong to an exclusive customer club in order to use-- had stopped working. I called customer service.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "That's right," I was told after a lengthy hold. "The machine is still under warranty." It would be picked up for repair within three working days.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: In the meantime, while I was waiting for the coffee machine, I realized that the plaster wall and paint job had morphed into a replacement of old doors, installation of an entirely new air conditioning system called something like Inventor, and the sudden urgent need for a new bedroom set whose size would be compatible with the modern design. "Adjustable, " my wife called it.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: The interior designer also suggested moving the piano to a different location, and building an acoustic wall that would contain the sound. And he proposed that I please put some life into my anemic study. And I agreed, even though I didn't understand exactly what that meant.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: His iPad has a calculator, and a few quick clicks produced the sum of more than 100,000 shekels, not counting the shoe closet. It took me a moment to recall that I had intended to spend no more than 20,000 shekels. I lapsed into depression, because I had already made the down payment and because I didn't want to tell my wife that we might not be able to meet the future payments. So I said nothing, and she gave me a designer smile such as I hadn't seen for a few years.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: A few days later, on the day when we were supposed to get our prestigious coffee machine back from repairs between 5:00 and 7:00 PM, she said, "Do you  know what's most unsuited to my needs in this apartment?" "Yes," I said. "All the inconvenient things. But everything is going to be fine."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "No," she said. "I think I'm deceiving myself with all this new design and renovation."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I don't understand," I said, genuinely not understanding.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "What bothers me the most," she said, "is that since we've moved here, you haven't wanted to barbecue. I so much want you to barbecue like we used to back in the village every Friday."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Barbecue?" I felt my blood pressure rising. "I'm going to spend $100,000 shekels for an interior designer and all you really want is a barbecue?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Well," she said, "I miss the village. And the days when you weren't embarrassed to barbecue next to the neighbors." At that point, the phone rang.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Hello," the voice on the phone said as I started to foam at the mouth. "I'm from the delivery company. I have a coffee machine for you. What's the address?" he asked in Arabic.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I gave him the address. He was silent for a while. And then he said, "But I only deliver in East Jerusalem. I'm sorry. I was told you were an Arab."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "You know what?" I replied in Arabic, "Forget it. I don't want the espresso machine. I don't even like that kind of coffee."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: November 22, 2012. The renovations have begun. The apartment is in chaos and I've decided that I'm going to buy the most comfortable bed I can find, and this time I won't even look at the price.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I picked up my wife from work and we went to buy the bed of our dreams. "We want the most comfortable bed you have in the store," I declared to the saleswoman who approached us with a smile.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Of course," she said, leading us to the area of the double beds. "Are you interested in an adjustable bed?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Only adjustable," I declared festively. And the polite saleswoman smiled once again and accompanied us to the area of the adjustables.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Ah," I sighed as I sprawled on the mattress and closed my eyes.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "We also have it in 6 and 1/2 feet wide."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "6 and 1/2 feet, hmm." I said to the saleswoman. "Exactly how much does the same bed cost in that size?" When she told me, I shouted. "How much?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I'll ask the store manager. Maybe he can give you a better price," she said.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "That's insane," I said to my wife when the saleswoman went to call the manager. "All that money for what? For foam, a few springs, and the remote control of a toy racing car?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "You said you didn't care about the price," she said. "Why do you even bother making declarations like that?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Why? Did I think those were going to be the prices? I was willing to waste up to 5,000 shekels. And I thought that for 4,000 shekels, I would be able to get the best mattress on the market."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Well, apparently this is the real price of mattresses," she said.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Shalom," said the store manager, who came up to us with an amazingly wide smile. He introduced himself and offered his hand, and I introduced myself when I shook his hand.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Pleased to meet you, 'Sa-eed,'" he continued in Hebrew, mispronouncing my name. I didn't correct him. Neither did my wife.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: He was quite nice, the manager, despite the prices he was asking. And he had a slight speech problem. He spoke very slowly, emphasizing each letter and nodding his head after every word.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: (SPEAKING SLOWLY) "You know about this mattress?" he asked, naming the brand that every child in Israel is familiar with.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Yes," I replied in the same vein out of politeness, so he wouldn't think, god forbid, that my fast speech was meant to mock him. (SPEAKING SLOWLY) "We've heard about that mattress."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "So you know which store you've come to?" He smiled and nodded.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Yes," I answered, and nodded too, smiling slowly.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I liked him, that manager. I also liked the chain for not hesitating to hire a manager with a speech impediment. I was already thinking of buying the mattress, although I had planned to spend a quarter of that amount. But it would be worth it to support a business whose owners are, first of all, human beings.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: Suddenly he stopped talking to answer the cellphone that was ringing in his pants pockets. "Hello!" he answered with a speed that left me and my wife amazed. "Moshe, I'll get back to you in 15 minutes. [INAUDIBLE]. Bye." And he hung up.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: (SPEAKING SLOWLY) "So where were we?" he continued slowly while nodding. I looked at my wife, who looked back at me. "Ah yes," he said. "The mattress."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Listen," I said to him at top speed. "Listen, we know what this damn mattress is. Do you understand?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Yes," he answered in a panic. "But why are you angry?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Because we may be Arabs," I answered irritably, "but we aren't idiots!"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "God forbid!" apologized the manager, putting his hand on his chest. "I definitely didn't mean that! I really didn't. I'm sorry if that's how it seemed to you!"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: My wife took her bag and decided that we weren't buying anything from someone like him. "Not on your life!" I said as we started making our way out of the store. "Racist idiot!"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Wait!", he chased after us. "I apologize!"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Forget it," I answered firmly. "We're not doing business with someone like you!"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I'll give you a big discount," he pleaded.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Forget about it," said my wife. "It's not a matter of discount. It's a matter of principle."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Look, I'll take off 25%. What do you say?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I said no," said my wife, with the determination of a social worker who believes that a principle is a principle.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I'll give it to you for half price!" insisted the manager, who really was sorry that he had spoken slowly.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Principles are principles," continued my wife on her way out of the store, while I stopped in my tracks.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Half price? Are you serious?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I swear," he said. "And I've never done that for anyone, but I really didn't intend to insult you."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Sayed!" my wife shouted at me. "Where are your values?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Forget values," I told her as I shook the hand of the nice salesman. "The man told you (SPEAKING SLOWLY) half price. Do you understand?" And with tears in his eyes, the salesman said that he would also give us pillows at a big discount.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: December 6, 2012. It's been three weeks of renovation and we've started moving back into our apartment, even though it's still not completely finished. When we got there, two Arab workers from a company that specializes in cleaning renovated houses were toiling in the rooms.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I felt uncomfortable at having Arabs cleaning my place, but I just nodded and told the contractor who was supervising the renovation that everything was packed and in the car. And that as soon as he gives the go ahead, I will start taking in the suitcases and bags.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: Besides the cleaners, the installer of the banister was also supposed to come. "Two hours of work," the contractor said. "He won't interfere with the cleaners and the cleaners won't interfere with him."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: The banister guy arrived exactly on time. "This is Sayed," the contractor said as he introduced me. The man nodded and smiled.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Great, Sayed. There might be sparks, so I want you to follow me with a brush and fix up after me."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "No," the contractor said, embarrassed. "He's the owner."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Ah," the installer said, and got to work.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "You know," my wife said to me on that sleepless night before the move back, "the house is really charming now. It looks prestigious and comfortable. But still--" she stopped.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Still what?" I asked.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I don't know," she said, as she always does when she knows. "I'm just thinking about the children again. About what this is doing to them. How they feel. How it will affect their behavior and the way they get along."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Again the thing with the Jewish neighborhood?" I said.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I'm not saying anything," she said. "It's a lovely apartment. Very nice neighbors. But you know."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "No. I absolutely, absolutely do not know," I replied with the jangled nerves of someone who had planned to spend only 20,000 shekels to add a room with a plaster wall, but found himself paying, as of that moment, more than 180,000 shekels.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I'm just asking myself," she said, striking a dramatic pose so the words would sink in. "I'm just asking myself if this is our natural place. And even more so for the children."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "It is natural," I said. "It's 100% natural."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: The banister guy came up to me smiling. "I hope you'll excuse me," he said. "I just, I never imagined that you live here. You know what I mean, Sayed."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Sure," I said. "Sure, forget it." And I really meant that, because it didn't hurt me in the least that he thought I was an Arab laborer. At least it didn't hurt me as much as the fact that I had two Arab workers doing their thing in my apartment and I had tried to avoid contact with them until one of them came over and spoke to me in Hebrew.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "These shoes were thrown out," said the worker, who I estimated was my father's age. "They were in the garbage. Can I have them for the kids?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I choked up for an instant, not sure whether to smile, reply in Hebrew, and play the generous Jewish homeowner who takes pity on the wretches, or to answer in Arabic and come across as a maniac Arab who lives among Jews and throws out almost-new Nikes that were brought from the US in the wrong size for the kids. I found myself saying, [ARABIC] "Please, go ahead," in Arabic. And continuing in Arabic, "Of course you can take them. And there are plenty more we had planned to donate if you want to have a look."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Your Arabic is excellent," the worker said, still speaking in Hebrew.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I am an Arab," I declared.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: The worker did a double take and asked, "And this is your place?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Yes," I told him. "We bought it a few years ago. Yes, this is my home."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Wella," he said, still amazed. "I never imagined. [FOREIGN LANGUAGE], thank you."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "For what?" I said. I didn't understand what he was thanking me for and I thought for a moment he was teasing me.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "The shoes," he said, holding them up with one hand to show me.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "You're welcome," I said. My face burned with shame.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: I talked to my wife late that night after the children were asleep. "What can I do?" I said leaning back a little in my bed. "And what exactly is our natural place? What?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I don't say it's easy," she said, invoking her social work phrases again. "It can be very hard."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "So are you telling me that I have to live in an Arab village to feel I'm in a natural place?" I asked. "I'm not allowed city life?"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "That's not what I'm saying," she said with a patience that I was quickly losing.

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Then what are you saying?" I insisted. "I really want to understand. What are my options for being natural? Hmm? To buy a crappy apartment in an Arab neighborhood in Jerusalem? To buy a place in the area that was conquered in 1967?

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: What, what is natural? To go back to the village? Back to Tira to the family? To fights between siblings over every meter of land? What is natural?

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: And what can I do in order to safeguard the children? You tell me that, please! What is right and what is wrong? And I will do it!"

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "I say you should go to sleep now," she said, rubbing cream into her hands and yawning. "You look tired."

segments.speaker: Sayed Kashua
segments.text: "Yes," I said. "Goodnight." And I knew I would not sleep soundly. Or wake up naturally.
